papers.title: Importance of the Quality of TME in Rectal Cancer Resection-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Kastner C, Hendricks A, Wagner J, Müller S, Uttinger K, Flemming S
papers.abstract: Retrospective studies and analyses of RCTs showed that surgical quality of mesorectal excision affects oncological outcomes of rectal cancer patients. Objective of this study was to determine the impact of mesorectal excision quality on local recurrence and overall survival in rectal cancer patients. MEDLINE was searched till April 1, 2024, with MeSH terms: rectal cancer/neoplasm, total mesorectal excision, TME, rectal cancer surgery, macroscopic assessment/evaluation, quality/adequacy/completeness of surgery/mesorectum/resection specimen, prognosis, and outcome for randomized clinical trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies reporting oncological outcomes and quality of the mesorectal excision. The main outcome and measures were local recurrence and overall survival. TME quality was classified into three grading categories (complete or mesorectal resection (MRR); nearly complete or intramesorectal resection (IMR); incomplete or muscularis propria resection (MPR)). Of 438 records screened and an additional three studies by cross-referencing, 15 articles with 11,285 individual patients were identified. Median age of included patients was 63, 55 (range 21, 0-95, 0). Pooled incidence of good (MRR), intermediate (IMR), and insufficient (MPR) TME quality was 65, 6%, 22, 8%, and 11, 6%, respectively. Insufficient TME quality was associated with locally advanced tumors. No difference in TME quality was observed between patients with and without neoadjuvant therapy. Pooled analysis showed lower odds for LR and higher odds for OS in patients with good TME quality, which is also shown in a subgroup analysis of neoadjuvantly treated patients. In conclusion, this meta-analysis confirms that good TME quality is associated with lower risk for local recurrence and higher probability for overall survival, an association that persisted also in neoadjuvantly treated patients. These findings suggest that neoadjuvant therapy will not compensate for suboptimal surgical quality; however, given the substantial heterogeneity across the included studies and the limited availability of data on contemporary treatment regimens, they should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive.

papers.title: "Let them do it": surgeon proficiency level and outcomes after ostomy reversal: a single-center retrospective study and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Vaghiri S, Sultani A, Uerlichs H, Pandkhahi A, Elmaghraby E, Abdelsamad A
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ostomy reversal is a frequently performed procedure in colorectal surgery and is often considered suitable for surgical training. However, evidence regarding the impact of surgeon training level on postoperative outcomes remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate outcomes after ostomy reversal performed by residents versus consultant surgeons through a combined single-center analysis and systematic review with meta-analysis.
METHODS: A retrospective, single-center observational study was conducted, including 255 patients who underwent loop ileostomy or loop colostomy reversal between 2012 and 2024. Postoperative outcomes were compared between procedures performed by residents and consultants. The observational study was conducted and reported in accordance with STROBE guidelines. In addition, a systematic review and meta-analysis were carried out according to PRISMA guidelines to assess outcomes after loop ileostomy reversal stratified by surgeon training level. The primary outcomes were overall and major postoperative morbidity.
RESULTS: In the single-center cohort, postoperative outcomes after ostomy reversal were largely comparable between residents and consultants. Residents more frequently performed direct stoma closure and had shorter operative times, and their patients were discharged sooner. Major postoperative morbidity was significantly higher in consultant-performed ileostomy reversals, likely reflecting greater procedural complexity. The meta-analysis of available comparative studies, including 1,196 patients (resident: n = 419; consultant: n = 777), demonstrated that resident-performed loop ileostomy reversal was not associated with inferior outcomes. In contrast, resident-performed stoma reversal was associated with lower rates of overall postoperative morbidity (OR = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.46-0.76; p < 0.0001) and major postoperative morbidity (OR = 0.66; 95% CI, 0.44-0.99; p = 0.04), whereas complication-specific outcomes did not differ significantly between groups. Notably, serious risk of bias and low certainty of evidence were detected.
CONCLUSION: Resident-performed ostomy reversal appears safe and feasible when conducted within a structured and supervised training environment. Findings from both the single-center analysis and the meta-analysis support integrating stoma reversal procedures into surgical residency training.

papers.title: Tools for in vivo assessment of the intestinal epithelial barrier in inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review
papers.authors: Vieujean S, Atreya R, Buda A, Caradec J, Citi S, Danese S
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Epithelial barrier alterations contribute to the pathogenesis and progression of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Barrier healing may predict long-term outcomes more accurately than endoscopic, histological or even transmural healing, and persistent epithelial abnormalities despite mucosal healing may underlie residual symptoms. Reliable tools are therefore needed to determine whether this therapeutic goal has been achieved and to support the development of barrier-directed therapies. We systematically reviewed the methods available to assess intestinal epithelial barrier structure and function in IBD.
METHODS: MEDLINE and Scopus were searched to July 25, 2025, for studies assessing epithelial barrier structure or function in patients with IBD. Animal, in vitro and ex vivo studies, and those without a clearly described assessment method, were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data on tools, thresholds, and associations with disease activity, treatment and outcomes.
RESULTS: Of 12 307 records screened, 124 studies were included: 73 evaluated permeability probes, 30 endogenous biomarkers and 25 invasive techniques, with four studies assessing both permeability probes and endogenous biomarkers. Probe-based testing relies on urinary recovery of orally administered sugars, polyethylene glycols, iohexol, radiolabelled compounds or fluorophores. Biomarkers reflect epithelial injury, microbial translocation, or the host response to it. Invasive techniques allow real-time, segment-specific assessment, principally probe-based confocal laser endomicroscopy, whose scores predict relapse and major adverse outcomes; endocytoscopy combined with multispectral spatial imaging is an emerging alternative.
CONCLUSIONS: A broad range of functional, molecular and morphological tools is now available. Validating thresholds, standardising outcome measures and better defining barrier healing are the next steps before it can become a therapeutic target.

papers.title: A multicenter study of capsule endoscopy in preschool children in China
papers.authors: Jin M, Mi M, Gong Y, Liao W, Chen J, Sun K
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety and clinical utility of capsule endoscopy in preschool-aged children.
METHODS: A multicenter retrospective study design was used, including data from eight specialized pediatric hospitals in China. Children aged < 6 years who were hospitalized and underwent capsule endoscopy between January 2020 and August 2025 were included.
RESULTS: This study included 155 patients (mean age 56.9 ± 14.2 months). The most common indication was chronic abdominal pain (50.97%), followed by suspected inflammatory bowel disease (22.58%), gastrointestinal bleeding (16.13%), and unexplained anemia (8.39%). Abnormal findings were identified in 69 cases, which established a definitive diagnosis in 55 patients (diagnostic yield, 35.5%), including 15 with isolated small-bowel disease. Capsule retention occurred in three patients with Crohn's disease. Fifty patients swallowed the capsule independently, while others required endoscopic placement; endoscopic assistance increased the success rate of capsule delivery to 100% in preschool children. When preschool children exhibited elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein(CRP) 6 mg/L [interquartile range (IQR), 0.81-23 mg/L] vs. 0.95 mg/L [IQR, 0.51-3.58 mg/L]; erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 16 mm/h [IQR, 6-27 mm/h] vs. 7 mm/h [IQR, 4-14 mm/h]), lower albumin levels (38.47 ± 8.83 g/L vs. 42.50 ± 4.92 g/L), and intestinal wall thickening on imaging (56.36% vs. 20.00%), the diagnostic positive rate significantly increased.
CONCLUSIONS: Capsule endoscopy is safe for preschool children. Capsule retention is mainly associated with underlying diseases. Capsule endoscopy is recommended to assess small-bowel lesions in children with elevated inflammatory markers, reduced albumin levels, or radiographic evidence of bowel wall thickening, facilitating early diagnosis and treatment.

papers.title: Clinical characteristics and oncological outcomes of upper tract urothelial carcinoma in patients with personal or family history of Lynch-syndrome-associated cancers
papers.authors: Manivasagam S, Truong H, Hensley P, Matin S, Ungerer G, Potretzke A
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) is a rare malignancy with complex clinical behavior, particularly in patients with hereditary cancer syndromes such as Lynch syndrome. In the absence of universal tumor testing for mismatch repair deficiency or microsatellite instability, personal or family history of Lynch syndrome-associated cancers (PFHLAC) may serve as a surrogate marker for identifying patients at risk. This study aims to characterize the clinical features and oncological outcomes of UTUC in patients with PFHLAC.
METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study of 1,893 patients who underwent radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) for UTUC between February 2000 and February 2021 across 7 U.S. institutions. Patients were stratified based on the presence or absence of PFHLAC. Clinical, pathological, and treatment-related variables were compared. Oncologic outcomes (bladder recurrence, extravesical recurrence, all-cause mortality, and cancer-specific mortality) were modeled using Cox proportional hazards with adjustment for clinical, surgical, and pathologic covariates.
RESULTS: Of the total cohort, 223 patients (11.7%) had PFHLAC. These patients were younger at surgery (70 years vs. 72 years, P < 0.001), more likely to be female (45.3% vs. 32.1%, P < 0.001), and exhibited higher rates of multifocal tumors (30.9% vs. 24.4%, P = 0.038), nodal involvement (cN1 or N2 11.5% vs. 10.7%, P = 0.031), and lymphovascular invasion (34.1% vs. 28.8%, P < 0.001). They frequently received neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) (32.3% vs. 19.4%, P < 0.001). On Cox modeling, PFHLAC was not associated with increased risk of recurrence or all-cause mortality but had lower risk of cancer-specific mortality (HR 0.59, P = 0.044).
CONCLUSIONS: UTUC in patients with PFHLAC demonstrates distinct clinical and pathological features, with reduced risk of cancer-specific mortality. Routine screening for Lynch syndrome using clinical criteria, immunohistochemistry, and confirmatory genetic testing may improve identification and management of high-risk patients. These findings support the need for personalized approaches and further prospective studies in this population.

papers.title: Targeting cancer immune evasion with anti-FOLR1 antibody-drug conjugate potentiates anti-PD-1 efficacy in colorectal cancer
papers.authors: Chen S, Liu Q, Ye S, Yu J, Xie Y, Yuan Y
papers.abstract: Loss of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) antigen presentation in tumor cells drives immune evasion and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in colorectal cancer (CRC). To identify therapeutic targets reversing this, we conducted fluorescence-activated cell sorting-based CRISPR activation screens using a druggable genome library and identified folate receptor α (FOLR1) as a top negative regulator. FOLR1 was heterogeneously expressed in CRC tumors but undetectable in adjacent normal tissues. High expression of FOLR1 predicted a poor ICB response, enhanced cancer stemness, and unfavorable patient outcomes. Functional assays showed that FOLR1 promoted CRC stemness-associated properties and fostered an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) with impaired CD8+ T cell infiltration and cytotoxicity, thereby driving tumor progression. Proteomic analyses revealed that FOLR1 stabilized the lactyltransferase AARS1 (alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1), which lactylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) at lysine-193 (K193), facilitating its interaction with TCPTP (T cell protein-tyrosine phosphatase) and inducing STAT1 dephosphorylation at tyrosine-701. Consequently, impaired STAT1 signaling down-regulated MHC-I and up-regulated MYC proto-oncogene protein (c-MYC), facilitating evasion of T cell surveillance and enhancing cancer stemness. The anti-FOLR1 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) mirvetuximab soravtansine (IMGN853) exhibited potent activity against FOLR1-positive CRC cells, reprogramming the TME to an immune-active status. Combining IMGN853 with anti-PD-1 (programmed cell death protein-1) therapy boosted antitumor immunity, sensitized tumors to immunotherapy, and induced robust tumor regression in vivo. Our findings support anti-FOLR1 ADC as a clinically actionable approach to overcome immune evasion and unlock immunotherapy efficacy in CRC.

papers.title: Tertiary lymphoid structures in luminal gastrointestinal cancers: biological circuits, spatial architecture, and biomarkers in the perioperative immunotherapy era
papers.authors: Sun S, Chen J, Zhong Y, Luo Y, Zhang G
papers.abstract: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) are inducible, organized lymphoid clusters that recapitulate key functions of secondary lymphoid organs within chronically inflamed tumor tissue. In colorectal, gastric, and esophageal cancers, the most common luminal gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies, surgical resection preserves the spatial relationship between TLS and the tumor core, invasive margin, and surrounding mucosa, making the resected specimen a uniquely informative anchor for studying antitumor immunity. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from human cohorts, single-cell and spatial genomics, and perioperative immunotherapy trials. We trace the developmental continuum from loose lymphocytic clusters to germinal center-bearing follicles, contrast germinal center-dependent humoral immunity with germinal center-independent B-cell responses, and examine how regulatory T and B cells can turn TLS into immunosuppressive niches. We then analyze proposed inductive circuits, including chemokine-stromal organization, microbial and mutational antigenic pressure, and innate immune sensing, and discuss how desmoplasia, mechanical compression, hypoxia, and metabolic competition may arrest TLS maturation. A tumor-by-tumor comparison of colorectal, gastric, and esophageal cancers shows that TLS density, maturity, and anatomic localization carry divergent prognostic information; and diffuse gastric cancer, peritoneal metastases, and chemoradiated esophageal tumors illustrate states of TLS disruption. We also appraise neoadjuvant checkpoint trials (NICHE, NICHE-2, NEONIPIGA, CheckMate 577, MATTERHORN), consider TLS as complements to TNM staging for adjuvant decision-making and as candidate correlates of pathologic response, and outline experimental strategies for TLS induction and the technical prerequisites for translating TLS into surgical biomarkers. We hypothesize that mature, margin-positioned TLS are promising development- and location-dependent markers of organized antitumor immunity, but routine clinical use awaits standardized, multicenter validation. We therefore propose a minimum reporting framework to accelerate this translation.

papers.title: Exploring preoperative prediction of conversion in minimally invasive colorectal cancer surgery using Swedish and Danish national register data
papers.authors: Afshari K, Grönkvist R, Pettersson J, Larsson C, Ehrencrona C, Rosenberg J
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Conversion of minimally invasive surgery often adds operative time and may lead to complications. The aim was to develop a preoperative prediction model for conversion and identify predictive risk factors in minimally invasive colorectal cancer resections, to be used in consideration and counselling preoperatively.
METHODS: An observational study based on data from national Swedish registries (CRCBaSE, 2019-2021). Logistic regression models were used to predict conversion, with variable selection based on statistical performance. Model discrimination, calibration, and uncertainty were evaluated using the Brier score, AUC, calibration plots, and bootstrap resampling. External validation was performed in the Danish Colorectal Cancer Registry (2016-2020).
RESULTS: Minimally invasive surgery was performed on 7,811 patients. Seven preoperative predictors were identified as risk factors of conversion: body mass index (BMI), clinical T stage, age, previous abdominal surgery, sex, robotic approach, and left-sided tumour location. Risk of conversion increased with advanced T stage, left-sided tumours, prior abdominal surgery, extremes of BMI, and age up to 80 years, whereas robotic surgery and female sex reduced the risk of conversion. A 7-variable model was created and achieved an AUC of 0.730 in the Swedish test set but demonstrated reduced discrimination and calibration on internal validation (AUC 0.681). External validation in a Danish national cohort confirmed consistent directions of the predictors but showed further reduced predictive performance (AUC 0.608).
CONCLUSIONS: Internal validation did not maintain adequate discrimination or calibration, and neither did the external validation. Several variables showed consistent associations with conversion and may be regarded as candidate predictors.

papers.title: Ferroptosis in Colorectal Cancer: Molecular Mechanisms, Microbial Crosstalk, and Traditional Chinese Medicine Therapeutic Strategies
papers.authors: Fan D, Ma X, Hao S
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common malignancy worldwide and poses a significant clinical challenge owing to its high morbidity and mortality rates. Despite ongoing improvements in comprehensive treatment regimens and early detection, the 5-year survival rate of patients has not substantially increased. Ferroptosis is a novel form of regulated cell death that is context dependent and can exert either tumor-suppressive or tumor-promoting effects depending on cellular context and microenvironmental factors. Its therapeutic induction must balance tumor-cell killing against potential effects on normal intestinal epithelium and ferroptosis-sensitive immune populations. Therefore, this review aimed to synthesize the molecular characteristics of ferroptosis and its regulatory mechanisms, focusing on the potential value of traditional Chinese medicine in targeting ferroptosis for the treatment of CRC. Our review suggests that targeting ferroptosis is a promising but context-dependent strategy requiring further validation.

papers.title: Organoids as Functional Models of Hepatic Tropism in Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastasis: From a Selective Hepatic Niche to Liver-specific Vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) is favored by portal anatomy but determined by a sequence of organ-selective bottlenecks: sinusoidal arrest, early survival, immune escape, metabolic accommodation, and growth-pattern-specific expansion. This Review integrates direct human CRLM evidence, mechanistic models, and organoid studies to define what is established, what remains inferential, and what next-generation models must test. Paired primary-tumor and liver-metastasis organoids preserve inter- and intrapatient heterogeneity and can reproduce selected chemotherapy responses, but epithelial-only cultures cannot model hepatic receptivity. Liver-containing systems should therefore be built as question-specific modules that add hepatocytes, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, hepatic stellate cells, Kupffer or recruited myeloid cells, extracellular matrix, and flow only when required by the hypothesis. We propose an evidence-linked experimental framework combining longitudinal single-cell transcriptomics, chromatin profiling, metabolomics, isotope tracing, spatial readouts, and perturbation-rescue experiments. Particular emphasis is placed on extracellular-vesicle-mediated premetastatic niche formation, clinically observed microenvironmental evolution, and context-dependent vulnerabilities such as vessel co-option and liver-restricted immune-metabolic dependencies. We also define minimum reporting and validation standards required before organoid results can influence clinical decisions. The central conclusion is that organoids become models of hepatic tropism only when liver context is treated as a controlled causal variable rather than as the site from which tumor epithelium was sampled.
